title: Grid Reference to Postcode Finder: NGR Lookup
description: Find the nearest UK postcode for an Ordnance Survey grid reference with the Grid Reference to Postcode Finder — via postcodes.io data. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a grid reference paced out on a paper map for a Cotswold barn converts to coordinates, and the finder returns the postcode the Royal Mail would recognise for that ground.
quick_answer: The Grid Reference to Postcode Finder takes an Ordnance Survey grid reference, converts it to coordinates, and returns the nearest UK postcode using postcodes.io data. Paste the reference and read the postcode — the bridge between the paper-map world of letters and digits and the delivery world of postal addresses.

body.t: A survey note gives a grid reference; the van needs a postcode for the satnav. This finder joins the two Britains — the reverse trip runs through the
Field reports recorded by grid reference get their postal line filled in for correspondence and invoicing.
A rural venue known by its map reference acquires the postcode guests' phones can navigate to.
Historic site files cite references; attaching the modern postcode makes the archive searchable by everyone else's tools.
A point in open fields has no postcode of its own — the finder returns the NEAREST postcode the data holds and labels it as such. Nearest is orientation, not a postal address for the field.
Grid references are OSGB36-flavoured; postcodes.io works in coordinates. The finder converts datum-aware — skipping that step is how naive tools land a field's postcode in the next parish.

The nearest postcode, possibly a lane or farm away
The geographically nearest — boundaries are delivery rounds, not fences

popular_table.note: Postcodes identify delivery points (typically around 15 addresses per full postcode, varying widely) — they were never designed as area codes, and this finder treats them accordingly.

faq: Whose postcode data does it use?
postcodes.io — the open service built on the Office for National Statistics and Royal Mail-derived open data. Its record is the finder's record.
A postcode for a mountain summit?
The nearest valley postcode is what exists to return — labelled nearest. Summits do not receive post, and the finder does not pretend otherwise.
Old postcodes vanish from current data; a historic address's code may return its successor area instead.
In towns, metres to a street away; in sparse country, it can be a kilometre or more — the finder reports the postcode, and the map shows you the gap.
Can I use the postcode for navigation?
Yes — that is its best use. For a formal address, pair it with the street and locality from the map record.
Large organisations hold dedicated postcodes; a point inside one can return that code — correct, if occasionally surprising.
